183.t: Father and uncle, acrobats and brass players, and getting his first drum
183.s: His father (trombone) and uncle (trumpet) toured vaudeville with an acrobatic act and closed it with a duet; his father insisted on study before a trumpet, so Watts took the drum and rehearsed with them.
183.q: Well, my dad and my uncle. They was, you might say, my inspiration to start a musical career. What did they do? Well, they was tumblers, professional troopers traveling on the R.K. O. Sakers, you know, all over the country. See, they had acrobatic act. And of course my daddy, the final of the act…

297.t: Other family musicians and Sonny Henry's help
297.s: No family musicians besides an uncle with trumpet; Sonny Henry helped informally, and he studied about two years with Gaspard.
297.q: He never had to play to nobody.

262.s: His musical family led him to take trumpet lessons.
262.q: Well my father was a musician and uh, he played music through the years. As a matter of fact my family, you know, all were musically inclined and practically everybody in the family played some type of musical instrument. And actually when I grew up I sort of became a part of me.

619.t: Violin at nine, then piano with his sister
619.s: He started on violin, disliked it, took piano at twelve with his sister, and gave it up for his father's trade.
619.q: Nine when I was taking violin. Oh nine. Nine years old. Then when I got around twelve I started taking piano with my sister. She plays piano.

1054.t: Growing up with jazz, her father's piano and records
1054.s: Jazz was all around her; her father played piano, had other musicians in and kept a good record collection.
1054.q: Naturally I always liked it because my father had a great deal to do with it and he played it more so than any other kind of music and so it just became more or less part of me.

314.s: He played his first concert at six, was steeped in his father's pianist circle, quit music after his father died when he was 13, and studied with the Levines.
314.q: Well yeah eventually. But the classical thing went very deep. I mean I played my first concert when I was six — Mendelssohn and Beethoven and Josquin and Bach. And I concertized quite frequently. My father was a pianist and he knew all the great pianists. He knew a lot of the great opera singers…

397.t: Deciding at eleven to be a musician; violin and Nat King Cole
397.s: His father brought home Nat King Cole and Glenn Miller albums; he was studying violin but heard the music he loved.
397.q: That was early. That was early, during my childhood. I decided that I wanted to be a musician when I was eleven years old. When I was eleven years old my father came to our apartment with two albums, one by the Nat King Cole Trio and the second one was the Glenn Miller Orchestra with Gene Krupa on…

323.t: Father starts him on clarinet when the family moves to Thomas
323.s: No radio at home; his clarinetist father gives him a clarinet and he practices happily on his own.
323.q: Oh God, no we didn’t have a radio. No. First it was my father. My father was a very good clarinetist. Not great like today, you know. Today they’ve gotten better and better and better. Like saxophones and flutes and oboes and whatever. We have progress, the instruments, it’s amazing what we are…

693.t: Buying a cheap guitar and winning over his parents
693.s: He saves for a twenty dollar guitar, struggles to play along with records, then wows a dinner party with a friend's concertina. His mother later objects when he gets serious.
693.q: piano. You know, and so forth. And maybe that’s what he thought, I don’t know. So anyway, I sort of got a guitar, I saved up my money doing errands and allowance and jobs and things like that, and I went to New York and got like a twenty dollar guitar, a terrible thing, I didn’t know any better,…

330.t: Practicing in the barn and Tommy Flanagan opening his eyes to jazz
330.s: Winter practice in the barn, a piano at about eleven, and meeting Tommy Flanagan at Northern High School.
330.q: No, no, no. They said you want to bang on it? Bang on it out in the barn. And I did, winter and spring and summer and fall I’d go out there. I got so good I used to cut the fingers off my gloves in the wintertime, and put my coat around my neck and go out and play, and practice that piano. I’d get…

520.t: Growing up in Detroit: piano, drums and cousin Clarence Stamps
520.s: Musical parents, abandoning piano for drums, and his cousin Clarence Stamps teaching him.
520.q: Yes it really was. My father played piano and drums, and my mother played piano. And I started out playing piano, actually started out with playing piano. Most kids started out playing — because the piano is in the homes mostly. So I did that for a while. But the piano to me was, at five or six, it…

562.t: Learning standards with her jazz-guitarist father before classical lessons
562.s: She started jazz first, playing standards nightly with her father from age five; classical lessons began at seven to build her instrument skills.
562.q: Dad was a jazz guitarist. So although he was just, he just did it for fun, once the kids started coming along, we played every night after dinner from age five on. And so actually my lessons started at age seven as a support to having learned standards with Dad. I could play the real easy kind of…

696.t: Getting his first trumpet at nine and learning from his father
696.s: Parents surrounded him with music and art; he got a trumpet at nine, shelved it, then secretly played from his father's books in high school.
696.q: Right. Well they encouraged me in the way that they presented me the home that I grew up with with all of that. Because my father was a visual artist as well and my uncles were visual artists. So I had all that around me. I was seeing that, I was into music, seeing all the drawings and the…

789.t: Piano, organ and rock bands before harmonica
789.s: He started piano at eight, studied classical piano at Manhattan School of Music, played pipe organ and rock, and took up harmonica at 18.
789.q: Well I started out on piano when I was eight. I studied classical piano at the Manhattan School of Music for four years on Saturdays, for four years. And so I was playing piano. And then I studied the pipe organ. I went to a private school that had a pipe organ. I did that for two years. I played a…

749.t: Deciding at eleven or twelve to make music her life's work
749.s: She had played piano six or seven years, accompanying herself, before deciding to pursue music as a profession.
749.q: I can recall the first time I knew that it was going to be my life’s — the goal, and that it was going to be my life’s work but I didn’t know necessarily that I was going to be a musician. I was already a musician when I decided that, that I was going to make it my profession. I was already a…

423.t: How he got his first drum set
423.s: His Teamster father took a bass and snare drum as payment for a $20 loan and carried them home on the subway; he had played piano for years but did not love it.
423.q: Oh, my first drum set? Yeah I guess you know the story. My dad, who was a Teamster, he worked on the docks, he had loaned $20 to somebody, and the fellow was up against it, he couldn’t give him the $20, and he said to my dad, “doesn’t your son like music?” Because at the time I was playing piano. I…

618.t: Earliest music and improvising at the Steinway
618.s: A Steinway was in the house from birth; he improvised from age two or three and his parents shielded him from formal study until seven.
618.q: It must have been something at home because there was a Steinway piano in the house from the day I was born and before. And so I imagine what I first heard was one of my parents playing the piano or playing some 78 recording of some classical music. That’s
